docs.title: Workflow Steps
docs.text:
Workflow steps are Python functions that Titan can execute from a workflow.

This page explains how to write them, how they receive and return data, and when to use each kind of step source.

docs.title: What a step function looks like
docs.text:
Every step function follows the same basic signature:

from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error, Skip, Exit


def my_step(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    return Success("Done")

The function name must exactly match the step: value used in YAML.

# .titan/steps/run_linter.py
def run_linter(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    ...

- plugin: project
  step: run_linter

docs.title: Where steps can come from
docs.text: Step source YAML form Typical use Plugin step plugin: git, plugin: github, plugin: jira Reuse built-in or plugin-provided capabilities Project step plugin: project Repository-specific Python logic User step plugin: user Personal reusable steps in ~/.titan/steps/ Core step plugin: core Built-in Titan helpers

docs.title: Reading data from the workflow context
docs.text:
Use ctx.get(...) to read values from the current workflow context.

branch_name = ctx.get("branch_name")
draft = ctx.get("draft", False)

Those values can come from:

  • workflow params
  • step params
  • metadata returned by earlier steps

docs.title: Returning data to later steps
docs.text:
There are two ways to make values available to later steps:

  • ctx.set("key", value) while the step is running
  • metadata={...} on Success(...) or Skip(...)

Both end up in the workflow context. In practice, project and plugin steps often use ctx.set(...) while building up values during the step, then return a plain Success(...) at the end.

ctx.set("branch_name", "feat/search")
return Success("Branch created")

Later steps can then read that value with ctx.get("branch_name").

docs.title: Result types
docs.text:
Step functions return one of these result types:

from titan_cli.engine import Success, Skip, Error, Exit

docs.title: Success
docs.text: Use when the step completed successfully.

docs.title: Skip
docs.text: Use when the step had nothing to do, but the rest of the workflow should continue.

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Use when the step failed.

docs.title: Exit
docs.text:
Use when the whole workflow should stop early in a controlled way.

If cleanup steps still need to run, prefer Skip over Exit.

docs.title: A minimal project step
docs.text:
import subprocess

from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error


def run_tests(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    result = subprocess.run(["pytest"], capture_output=True, text=True)

    if result.returncode != 0:
        return Error("Tests failed")

    return Success("Tests passed")

docs.title: A step that passes data forward
docs.text:
from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error


def choose_branch(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    branch_name = ctx.get("branch_name")
    if not branch_name:
        return Error("Missing branch_name")

    ctx.set("selected_branch", branch_name)
    return Success("Branch selected")

docs.title: When to use a command step instead
docs.text:
Use a command step when:

  • the action is a straightforward shell command
  • no custom Python branching is needed
  • no ctx.textual UI interaction is needed
  • no reusable Python logic is being introduced

Use a project step when:

  • you need Python conditionals or parsing
  • you want to pass structured metadata to later steps
  • you want to use ctx.textual
  • the command version would be awkward or unsafe

docs.title: Using ctx.textual
docs.text:
If you want your step to look and feel like the rest of Titan, use ctx.textual.

That lets you:

  • show step headers and status
  • display formatted text, markdown, panels, and tables
  • ask for user input interactively
  • show loading indicators during long operations

See Textual in Steps for the public API.

docs.title: Using built-in clients inside steps
docs.text:
When Titan builds the workflow context, some steps can access ready-to-use clients directly from ctx.

Common examples:

  • ctx.git for Git operations
  • ctx.github for GitHub operations
  • ctx.jira for Jira operations
  • ctx.ai for AI-powered operations when AI is configured

Always check that the client you need is available before using it.

docs.title: Example: using ctx.git
docs.text:
from titan_cli.core.result import ClientSuccess, ClientError
from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error


def show_git_status(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    if not ctx.git:
        return Error("Git client is not available")

    result = ctx.git.get_status()

    match result:
        case ClientSuccess(data=status):
            ctx.set("git_status", status)
            return Success("Git status loaded")
        case ClientError(error_message=err):
            return Error(f"Failed to get git status: {err}")

Typical use cases:

  • inspect repository state
  • get the current branch
  • create commits or push branches

docs.title: Example: using ctx.github
docs.text:
from titan_cli.core.result import ClientSuccess, ClientError
from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error


def fetch_pull_request(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    if not ctx.github:
        return Error("GitHub client is not available")

    pr_number = ctx.get("pr_number")
    if not pr_number:
        return Error("Missing pr_number")

    result = ctx.github.get_pull_request(int(pr_number))

    match result:
        case ClientSuccess(data=pr):
            ctx.set("pr_info", pr)
            return Success("Pull request loaded")
        case ClientError(error_message=err):
            return Error(f"Failed to fetch PR: {err}")

Typical use cases:

  • fetch PR or issue data
  • create pull requests or issues
  • request reviews or submit review actions

docs.title: Example: using ctx.jira
docs.text:
from titan_cli.core.result import ClientSuccess, ClientError
from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error


def load_jira_issue(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    if not ctx.jira:
        return Error("Jira client is not available")

    issue_key = ctx.get("jira_issue_key")
    if not issue_key:
        return Error("Missing jira_issue_key")

    result = ctx.jira.get_issue(key=issue_key)

    match result:
        case ClientSuccess(data=issue):
            ctx.set("jira_issue", issue)
            return Success("Jira issue loaded")
        case ClientError(error_message=err):
            return Error(f"Failed to fetch Jira issue: {err}")

Typical use cases:

  • load issue details
  • search issues with JQL
  • transition issues or assign fix versions

docs.title: Pattern to follow
docs.text:
When using built-in clients in steps:

  1. check that the client exists on ctx
  2. read required inputs from ctx.get(...)
  3. call the client method
  4. handle ClientSuccess and ClientError
  5. return Success, Skip, or Error with useful metadata for later steps

If your step also needs a consistent UI, combine this pattern with Textual in Steps.

docs.title: Built-in core steps
docs.text:
Titan also exposes built-in reusable steps through plugin: core.

These are not tied to a specific plugin like Git or GitHub. Use them when Titan already provides a generic capability directly.

docs.title: ai_code_assistant
docs.text:
Launches an external AI coding assistant CLI with context collected earlier in the workflow.

Typical use cases:

  • after linting to help fix remaining lint errors
  • after test failures to help diagnose or propose fixes
  • after a validation step that stores machine-readable output in ctx.data

Example YAML:

- id: ai-help-tests
  name: "AI Help - Tests"
  plugin: core
  step: ai_code_assistant
  params:
    context_key: "step_output"
    prompt_template: "Help me fix these failing tests:\n\n{context}"
    ask_confirmation: true
    fail_on_decline: false

Supported params:

  • context_key: required key in ctx.data to read context from
  • prompt_template: prompt template using {context} placeholder
  • ask_confirmation: ask the user before launching the assistant
  • fail_on_decline: return Error instead of Skip if the user declines
  • pre_launch_warning: optional warning text shown just before the CLI starts

Which CLI runs is not a step param, and nothing is asked mid-run. By default it is the CLI chosen once in AI Configuration → CLI (or with F2 from any screen, where M picks its model in the same pass and nothing is written until you accept). A user who wants this one task on a different CLI or model pins it on its row under AI Configuration → AI per task, and S in the F2 picker overrides both for the current session only. The same row routes the task to Off, in which case the step skips.

Behavior:

  • returns Skip if there is no context under context_key
  • returns Skip if no supported assistant CLI is installed at all
  • returns Skip if the user turned this task off
  • returns Error if required params are missing or invalid
  • returns Error if no default CLI is configured, or the configured one is not installed
  • returns Error if the launched CLI exits with a non-zero code
  • returns Success when the assistant exits successfully

Notes:

  • The step clears the consumed context_key from ctx.data after reading it, so later steps do not accidentally reuse stale context.
  • This step uses Titan's Textual UI and temporarily suspends the TUI while the external CLI runs.

docs.title: Recommended structure for public plugin steps
docs.text:
If you are exposing a public step from a plugin through get_steps(), treat it as part of the plugin's public API.

Use a canonical docstring structure:

def my_public_step(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    """
    One-line summary.

    Requires:
        ctx.github: An initialized GitHubClient.

    Inputs (from ctx.data):
        pr_number (int): Pull request number to inspect.

    Outputs (saved to ctx.data):
        pr_info: The fetched pull request object.

    Returns:
        Success: If the step completes successfully.
        Error: If required context is missing or execution fails.
    """

This is especially important for public plugin docs and generated step inventories.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• function name does not match step: in YAML
  • using Exit when Skip is the right result
  • forgetting to return metadata that later steps need
  • using a Python step for logic that could just be a simple command step
  • writing custom UI output instead of using ctx.textual

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Workflows
  • Textual in Steps
  • Your First Workflow

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
Titan workflows are YAML files that automate a sequence of actions: plugin steps, project steps, shell commands, and even other workflows.

This page explains the workflow model from a user point of view: what kinds of workflows you can create, what kinds of steps they can contain, and how they fit together.

docs.title: What a workflow is
docs.text:
A workflow is a sequence of steps executed in order.

Typical examples:

  • run checks, then create a commit
  • gather input, generate content with AI, then create a GitHub issue
  • create a worktree, do review work, then clean it up

A minimal workflow looks like this:

name: "Run tests and commit"
description: "Run tests, then create a commit"

steps:
  - id: run-tests
    name: "Run Tests"
    command: "pytest"

  - id: create-commit
    name: "Create Commit"
    plugin: git
    step: create_commit

docs.title: Workflow types
docs.text: There are several ways to use workflows in Titan.

docs.title: 1. New workflow from scratch
docs.text:
Create a brand new YAML file and define the full sequence yourself.

Use this when you want a custom automation that does not naturally extend an existing workflow.

docs.title: 2. Extended workflow
docs.text:
Extend another workflow and inject your own steps into its hooks.

Use this when Titan or a plugin already gives you most of what you need.

name: "Commit with AI + Linter"
extends: "plugin:git/commit-ai"

hooks:
  before_commit:
    - id: run-lint
      name: "Run Linter"
      plugin: project
      step: run_linter

docs.title: 3. Nested workflow
docs.text:
Call another workflow as a step.

Use this when you want to compose larger flows from smaller reusable ones.

steps:
  - id: commit-first
    workflow: "commit-ai"

docs.title: Where workflows live
docs.text:
Titan discovers workflows from four sources.

Priority Source Location Typical use 1 Project .titan/workflows/*.yaml Project-specific automation shared with the repo 2 User ~/.titan/workflows/*.yaml Personal reusable workflows across projects 3 System Bundled with Titan CLI Built-in core workflows 4 Plugin Bundled with each plugin Workflows shipped by plugins

Higher priority wins when two workflows have the same name.

That means a project workflow can override a plugin workflow simply by using the same filename and workflow name.

docs.title: Workflow structure
docs.text:
name: "My Workflow"
description: "What it does"

params:
  draft: false
  assignees: []

hooks:
  - before_commit
  - after_push

steps:
  - id: my_step
    name: "My Step"
    plugin: github
    step: create_pr
    on_error: continue
    params:
      draft: "${draft}"

Main fields:

  • name: human-friendly label shown in Titan
  • description: optional explanation
  • params: default values available through ctx.get(...)
  • hooks: named extension points other workflows can fill
  • steps: the ordered actions to run

docs.title: Step types
docs.text: Every workflow step must define exactly one action type.

docs.title: Plugin step
docs.text:
Calls a public step exposed by a plugin.

- plugin: github
  step: create_pr

Use this when the capability already exists in a plugin and you want to reuse it.

docs.title: Project step
docs.text:
Calls a Python step from .titan/steps/.

- plugin: project
  step: run_linter

Use this when the logic is specific to this repository.

docs.title: User step
docs.text:
Calls a Python step from ~/.titan/steps/.

- plugin: user
  step: my_global_helper

Use this for personal reusable automations across many projects.

docs.title: Core step
docs.text:
Calls a built-in Titan step.

- plugin: core
  step: ai_code_assistant

Use this when Titan already provides the generic behavior directly.

For the public built-in core step reference, see Workflow Steps.

docs.title: Command step
docs.text:
Runs a shell command.

- id: lint
  name: "Run Linter"
  command: "ruff check ."

Use this when the action is simple and you do not need custom Python logic or UI behavior.

docs.title: Nested workflow step
docs.text:
Runs another workflow.

- workflow: "commit-ai"

Use this when you want to compose workflows instead of repeating steps.

docs.title: Choosing the right step type
docs.text:
Use case Best fit Reuse a built-in plugin capability Plugin step Add project-specific Python logic Project step Reuse a personal helper across projects User step Use a Titan-provided generic helper Core step Run a straightforward command Command step Compose existing flows Nested workflow

For a full guide to writing Python steps and built-in core steps, see Workflow Steps.

docs.title: Parameters and variable substitution
docs.text:
Workflow-level params define defaults that all steps can read with ctx.get(...).

Step-level params are merged into the context before that step runs.

Use ${key} to interpolate values from the current context:

params:
  assignees: []

steps:
  - plugin: github
    step: create_issue
    params:
      assignees: "${assignees}"
      labels: "${labels}"

docs.title: Extending workflows with hooks
docs.text:
Hooks let you customize an existing workflow without copying the whole thing.

Base workflow:

name: "Commit with AI"
hooks:
  - before_commit

steps:
  - plugin: git
    step: get_status

  - hook: before_commit

  - plugin: git
    step: ai_generate_commit_message

  - plugin: git
    step: create_commit

Project extension:

name: "Commit with AI + Checks"
extends: "plugin:git/commit-ai"

hooks:
  before_commit:
    - id: run-lint
      name: "Run Linter"
      plugin: project
      step: run_linter

    - id: run-tests
      name: "Run Tests"
      command: "pytest"

Notes:

  • extends: "plugin:git/commit-ai" targets the base plugin workflow directly
  • extends: "commit-ai" resolves by precedence and may pick a project override
  • after is always available as an implicit hook at the end of a workflow

docs.title: Workflow resolution for nested workflows
docs.text:
There are two useful forms when calling another workflow:

# Use the highest-precedence workflow named commit-ai
- workflow: "commit-ai"

# Always call the base workflow shipped by the git plugin
- workflow: "plugin:git/commit-ai"

Use the prefixed form when you explicitly want the base plugin workflow and do not want a project override.

docs.title: Step result types
docs.text:
Every step returns one of four result types.

from titan_cli.engine import Success, Skip, Error, Exit
Result Meaning Success Step completed and workflow continues Skip Step had nothing to do and workflow continues Error Step failed; workflow stops unless on_error: continue Exit Stop the whole workflow early in a controlled way

docs.title: Success
docs.text:
return Success("Done")
return Success("Created branch", metadata={"branch_name": "feat/search"})

metadata is merged into ctx.data so later steps can reuse it.

docs.title: Skip
docs.text:
Use Skip when the step is not applicable, but later steps should still run.

return Skip("AI not configured")
return Skip("No labels to select")

docs.title: Error
docs.text:
Use Error when the step actually failed.

return Error("GitHub client not available")

In YAML, on_error controls whether the workflow stops or continues:

- plugin: project
  step: run_linter
  on_error: continue

docs.title: Exit
docs.text:
Use Exit when the whole workflow should stop cleanly because it is no longer needed.

return Exit("No changes to commit")

docs.title: Critical: Skip vs Exit
docs.text:
This is the most common mistake when writing workflow steps.

  • Skip means: this step has nothing to do, continue the workflow
  • Exit means: stop the whole workflow now

If resources have already been created, prefer Skip so cleanup steps can still run.

Wrong:

steps:
  - step: create_worktree
  - step: do_work
  - step: cleanup_worktree

If do_work returns Exit, cleanup_worktree never runs.

Safer pattern:

steps:
  - step: create_worktree
    on_error: continue

  - step: do_work
    on_error: continue

  - step: cleanup_worktree

And inside do_work, return Skip instead of Exit when there is simply nothing to do.

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Workflow Steps: how to write Python step functions
  • Textual in Steps: how to use ctx.textual for consistent TUI output
  • Your First Workflow: hands-on tutorial

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is a full screen dedicated to one service. Where a mod is a small pane that is always at hand, a workspace is where you work on the service: its own layout, its own shortcuts, its own data. You open it from its tile in the dock and leave it with Esc.

This page is for people who use workspaces. To write one, see Writing a Workspace.

docs.title: Workspaces, mods and plugins
docs.text:
What it is Where you see it Mod A summary that reacts to what Titan does Side panel, dock, home card, toasts Workspace The whole service on its own screen A dock tile that opens a full screen Plugin Clients, steps and workflows Inside workflows

A workspace and a mod are loaded the same way and can share a name: the github mod is the summary in the side panel (what needs you now), and its Open GitHub workspace button, or pressing one of its PRs or runs, opens the github workspace, with that row already unfolded.

docs.title: What Titan ships
docs.text:
Official plugins ship their workspaces, and they load while the plugin is enabled:

Workspace Plugin Shows github github The repo's pull requests (search, review, approve, merge, conflicts, check diagnosis), the merge queue and the latest workflow runs, in two columns that stack into one when the window is narrow

docs.title: Turning a workspace off
docs.text:
The Mods screen lists mods only. A workspace is switched by hand in ~/.titan/config.toml:

[workspaces.github]
enabled = false                # false turns it off everywhere

[workspaces.github.sections]
queue = false                  # switch one section off

[workspaces.github.options]
prs_refresh_seconds = 60       # override a declared option

An option value that does not fit its declared type, or an option the workspace never declared, is dropped with a warning in the log; the workspace gets its default.

docs.title: Where workspaces live
docs.text:
Same order as mods, the most personal winning when two share a name:

Order Source Folder 1 (widest) Titan titan_cli/workspaces/<name>/ 2 Plugin the plugin's workspaces_path 3 Project <repo>/.titan/workspaces/<name>/ — shared with the team 4 User ~/.titan/workspaces/<name>/ — yours 5 (most personal) Dev folders --workspace-dir <folder> or TITAN_WORKSPACE_DIRS, one workspace each

Workspaces are trusted code

A workspace runs inside Titan with your permissions; nothing sandboxes it. Committing one to .titan/workspaces/ shares it with everyone who runs Titan in that repository. Only load workspaces you would run as scripts.

A workspace that fails to parse, import or register is logged and left out whole; it never stops Titan from starting.

docs.title: Writing a Mod
docs.text:
A mod is a folder with two files:

~/.titan/mods/hello/
├── mod.toml     # what it is, what it needs, which events and slots it uses, its options
└── mod.py       # register(on, options)

Titan reads mod.toml without running anything, so a mod can be listed, explained and switched off before its code ever executes. For where to put the folder (yours, the team's, a plugin's) see Mods.

docs.title: A first mod
docs.text:
# mod.toml
[mod]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
icon = "👋"
description = "A pane that counts the workflows run this session"
events = ["app.start", "workflow.run", "ui.render"]
slots = ["pane"]

# mod.py
from titan_cli.ui.elements import Box, Button, Text


def draw(m, width):
    runs = m.state.get("runs", 0)
    return Box(
        Text(f"Workflows run: {runs}", bold=True),
        Button("Reset", lambda: m.state.set("runs", 0)),
        border="info",
    )


def register(on, options):
    @on("app.start")
    def start(m, e, next):
        m.ui.open("hello", "Hello")          # a pane in the side panel
        m.state.set("runs", 0)
        return next(e)

    @on("workflow.run")
    def counted(m, e, next):
        try:
            return next(e)
        finally:
            if not e.nested:
                m.state.update("runs", lambda n: n + 1)

    @on("ui.render", match={"component": "Pane", "pane": "hello"})
    def render(m, e, next):
        return draw(m, e.width)

Restart Titan with titan --mod-dir ~/code/hello, or drop the folder in ~/.titan/mods/. The folder is imported as the package titan_mod_<name>, with mod.py as its __init__, so a big mod splits into modules and imports them relatively (from .sections import prs).

docs.title: mod.toml
docs.text:
[mod]
name = "github"                       # letters, digits, _ and -, up to 64; must equal the folder name
version = "0.4.0"
icon = "⎇"                            # one character or emoji, on the rail, dock and home card
description = "..."
requires_plugins = ["github"]
events = ["app.start", "ui.render"]   # the only events register() may hook
slots = ["pane"]
ai_task = "PR check diagnosis"        # label of the AI routing task, if the mod uses m.ai
ai_assist_task = "Fix with AI"        # label of the help-button task, if it uses ai_assist_button

[options.refresh_seconds]             # typed, validated options
type = "int"                          # string | int | float | bool | list | choice
title = "Refresh every (s)"
default = 30                          # required
min = 1                               # int/float only; max too; choice takes `values = [...]`

[sections.queue]                      # a part the user can switch off
title = "Merge queue"
default = true
  • events is enforced. Hooking an event not listed makes register fail and the mod load not at all.
  • Options reach register as the options dict, defaults overridden by the user's [mods.<name>.options]. sections is reserved as an option name.
  • Sections reach the mod as options["sections"], a {name: bool}. Titan only keeps the switches: the mod decides what a switched-off section stops doing (polling, drawing).

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
register(on, options) hooks events with @on(event, match={...}). A hook is hook(m, e, next):

  • m is the mod's handle on Titan (below), e the event's frozen input.
  • next(e) runs the hooks below this one and then Titan's own behaviour, and returns its result. Call it at most once.
  • Return next(e) to observe, return something else to answer yourself, or pass dataclasses.replace(e, ...) to next to rewrite what the rest sees.
Event Input Fires Typical use app.start AppStart(project_root) The TUI has mounted Open panes, start timers, bind keys. Never block. workflow.run WorkflowRun(workflow, source, nested) Around a whole workflow React when it ends; outcome(result) reads the result as "success", "error", "skip" or "exit" step.call StepCall(workflow, step_id, step_name, plugin, step, command, nested_workflow, params) Around one step Guard (return m.deny("reason")) or rewrite params ui.render UIRender(component, pane, width) A slot is drawn Answer with an element tree section.change SectionChange(section, enabled) The user switches one of this mod's sections while Titan runs Start work when a section turns on

match filters on the event's fields: @on("ui.render", match={"component": "Pane", "pane": "hello"}).

Aborted workflows

A workflow the user aborts (Ctrl+C) never returns from next: it raises. A hook that must act however the run ends puts that code in a finally.

Hooks fail open

A hook that raises is logged and the chain carries on as if it had called next(e). There are no fail-closed guards and no per-hook time budget: a step.call guard that crashes lets the step run.

docs.title: The m API
docs.text:
Every hook receives the same m for its mod.

m.ui.open(pane, title) Give the mod a pane in the side panel, drawn by its ui.render hook m.ui.badge(pane, text, severity) Text under the pane's rail icon (three characters at most); None removes it w.ui.view, w.ui.open_workspace(name, focus), w.on_start, w.on_open Workspaces only. A workspace is a full screen with the same handle; a mod opens one with m.ui.open_workspace("github", focus={...}). See Writing a Workspace. m.ui.widget(name, cls) Bring your own widget: cls is a Textual widget with apply(props) (Updatable). A tree draws it with Component(name, props), and a redraw calls apply on the mounted widget, so its own state (focus, scroll) survives. name is global: prefix it with your mod's ("git.graph"). An unregistered name shows a line saying so. Titan removes it when the mod unloads. You accept the Textual coupling: Titan's Button, InputField and PressableRow are the catalog to copy from. m.ui.dock(label, badge, severity, on_click) A tile in the dock; None as label removes it m.ui.home_card(title, text, on_click) A card on the home screen; None removes it m.ui.toast(text, severity) information or warning. An error is never a toast: it opens an error card (a modal with a copy button), so use error_card in your pane when the error belongs there m.ui.copy(text, what) Copy to the clipboard and say so m.state get(key, default) / set / update(key, fn, default): in-memory values (default stands in for a missing key); every change repaints the mod's panes m.store get / set: small JSON values that survive the session (~/.local/state/titan/mods/<mod>.json) m.clock.every(seconds, fn, immediately=True) Run fn periodically on a background thread; a run still going is not doubled m.run(fn) Run fn once on a background thread m.client(name) The client of an installed, enabled plugin ("git", "github", "jira"), or None m.keys.bind(key, description, fn) App-wide key in Textual's spelling ("f5", "ctrl+k"); refused if Titan or another mod has it, returning False m.workflows.run(name, params) Open a workflow as if the user picked it, with params over its own; refused while another runs m.workflows.resolve(name) The workflow run(name) would open (a repo's extension of it, if any), or None when this Titan has none m.ai See AI m.deny(reason) The answer for a step.call hook that blocks a step m.log A structured logger bound to the mod

docs.title: Threading rules
docs.text:
Hooks, button handlers and key handlers run on the UI thread. Anything that waits goes elsewhere:

  • Network calls (m.client(...) methods) and AI calls (m.ai.complete) block: make them from a m.clock.every callback or inside m.run(...), never straight from a hook.
  • ui.render must read only m.state. It never waits on the network: a timer fills m.state, the render draws it.
  • Button on_press should be a state update, or hand slow work to m.run.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text: m.client("github") returns what steps see: methods returning ClientResult, matched with ClientSuccess / ClientError. A mod uses the plugin's operations and UI models too; it keeps no copy of them. If a plugin lacks something generally useful, it belongs in the plugin (with its docs), not in the mod.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
ui.render answers with a tree of plain values; Titan decides how to draw them. Mods never touch Textual widgets.

from titan_cli.ui.elements import Box, Button, Link, Text

Box(
    Text("PRs", bold=True, color="info"),
    Text(Link("#12", url), " fix the thing", Text(" · 2d", dim=True)),
    has_error and Text(err, color="error"),     # falsy children are dropped
    Button("Review", on_review, variant="primary"),
    border="info",
)
Element Notes Text(*parts, color, bold, dim, wrap) Parts are strings, Links or nested Text spans. Truncates with an ellipsis unless wrap=True. Link(label, url) Opens an http(s) URL. URLs in any text are links even when wrapped. Box(*children, border, row, indent, gap) Vertical group; border is a colour name; row=True puts children on one line: the first at the left, the rest pushed to the right (a title with a switch beside it). Columns(*children, ratio, gap), responsive_columns(width, builders, ratio, collapse_below, gap) Children side by side, each as wide as its share of ratio ((3, 2): three fifths and two fifths). responsive_columns is what to use in a ui.render or workspace view: each builder is called with the width its column has, so a choice_card fits either way, and under collapse_below columns (default 120) the builders stack in one column at the full width. Keep fields the user types in outside the columns: crossing the width rebuilds them. Button(label, on_press, dim, variant) With a variant (primary, default, success, warning, error) it is Titan's own button, for something that does work; without one it reads as a line of the pane, right for a fold or picker. label is a string, or a Text when parts of the line need their own style (a name plain, its date dim); a variant button flattens a Text to its words. error_card(message, copy=m.ui.copy, title, details, copy_text, what, actions, color) An ErrorCard: a bordered box with the error (wrapped, never cut off), its details dim and a "⧉ Copy error" button that puts it on the clipboard. actions are your own Buttons beside Copy (a "✦ Ask AI to fix", say); copy_text replaces what is copied. Import it from titan_cli.ui.components. Steps show the same card with ctx.textual.error_card(error, title, actions). choice_card(options, width, title, hint, state, key, close, border) A choice card: a bordered box that asks the user to pick, the standard way to offer actions to choose from. options are Option(label, on_press, variant); pass the width your ui.render received: options that sit together go on one line when they fit, in a grid of equal cells when they do not, and in a column when only one fits. Option(label, options=[...]) is a dropdown inside the card (▸/▾) and Option(label, content=Box(...), on_open=fn) one with a body of your own, such as a small form; state=m.state and key keep which one is open (one at a time; two cards in one pane need two keys) and close folds it after a pick. Mix options and dropdowns in one card instead of one card per kind. None options are dropped. Import Option and choice_card from titan_cli.core.mods. ai_assist_button(m, prompt, label, cwd) A help button for an error_card's actions or anywhere a Button goes: pressing it opens the user's interactive AI CLI with prompt typed in, through m.ai.assist. Which CLI and model is the user's choice in AI Configuration, on the task mods.<name>.assist (declare ai_assist_task in mod.toml so the AI screen lists it). No workflow in between; use a workflow only when the button must do more than open the CLI (check out a branch, commit, push). Import it from titan_cli.ui.components. fix_prompt(error, context) The prompt for "help me fix this error": the error whole, context after it (a log excerpt, the branch). Pass it to ai_assist_button. ask_ai(m, key, work) Asks the routed AI in the background and keeps the outcome under key as an AIResult (status running/done/error, text, model, error, and a free value for whatever work makes of the answer). work(m) calls m.ai.complete and returns its AIAnswer (or an AIResult). A second call under a key that is still running starts nothing and returns False. Read it with ai_result(m, key). ai_ask_button(m, key, work, label, again_label, running_label) The button that runs ask_ai; its label follows the state (ask, "… asking ", ask again). ai_answer_box(m, key, title, render) What key answered, with a copy button, or an error card; nothing while it runs or was never asked. render(value) draws the mod's own value instead of the text. ai_chip(m, title) The "⟳ who answers" line: pressing it opens m.ai.configure. Fill it at start with m.run(lambda: refresh_ai_chip(m)). Input(value, placeholder, on_change, on_submit, size) A text field: one line (size="compact", the default) or, with size="normal", three lines with a border, for a field that is the point of a screen such as a search box. on_change fires on every keystroke — keep it to an m.state update, never a network or disk call; on_submit (optional) fires on Enter, the right place to kick off a search or write to m.store. Component(name, props) A widget registered with m.ui.widget(name, cls), drawn with props. For what the elements above cannot say.

Colours are semantic: primary, accent, success, warning, error, info, subtle. Lists are flattened and falsy children (None, False, "", 0, []) dropped, so conditionals and comprehensions read naturally.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text:
Slot How Notes Side panel pane m.ui.open + ui.render Right of every screen; rail icon from mod.toml's icon, with m.ui.badge Dock tile m.ui.dock Bottom bar, always visible Home card m.ui.home_card Beside Quick launch Toast m.ui.toast One-off notification Key binding m.keys.bind Listed in the footer and in ?

The three visible slots are independent: a mod fills any mix, with different content in each (a count on the dock, detail in the pane, a summary and an action on the card). Titan's own prompts (ask_*) are never drawn by a mod, because their answer authorises an action.

docs.title: AI
docs.text:
m.ai.complete(prompt, system=None, max_tokens=None, model=None, timeout=180) returns an AIAnswer (.text, .model, .error, .ok). It goes through Titan's AI routing under the task mods.<name>: the user's connection or headless CLI, task pin, and F2/F3 for the session all apply. It blocks, so call it from m.run or a timer.

To let the user choose who answers, call m.ai.configure(title, on_done) from a button: it opens the same pickers as the AI screen and writes the task pin. m.ai.assist(prompt, cwd=None) returns an AssistResult (.opened, .reason): it resolves the task mods.<name>.assist (pinned like any task, and separate from mods.<name> because it is the one that may be an interactive CLI, which a one-shot complete could not run) and, when that is an interactive CLI, opens it with prompt typed in. It suspends Titan while the CLI runs, so call it from a button or key; a refusal (AI off, no CLI, a task that is not interactive) is already toasted, reason says why. m.ai.pinned() and m.ai.describe() say who answers now (describe may probe: call it off the UI thread). Declare ai_task (and ai_assist_task when the mod has a help button) in mod.toml so the AI screen lists each task with a readable label. Every AI call a mod makes goes through this routing: a mod never picks a CLI, a connection or a model itself.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: The same rules as steps: no Titan API returns a secret string, and a mod never keeps a raw secret in m.state, m.store or a pane.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Keep reading and drawing as plain functions over fake clients, and test them without mounting anything. import_mod imports a mod exactly as Titan does and ModBus().api(name) gives the m a hook receives:

from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from titan_cli.core.mods import ModBus, import_mod
from titan_cli.ui.elements import Text


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def mod():
    return import_mod(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent)


def test_draw_shows_the_count(mod):
    m = ModBus().api("hello")
    m.state.set("runs", 3)

    tree = mod.draw(m, 40)          # a plain function returning elements

    assert "Workflows run: 3" in tree.children[0].parts

To drive hooks, build a ModBus, give it a host with the methods your mod calls (bus.host = SimpleNamespace(...)), register with mod.register(bus.on_for("hello"), options) and fire events with bus.dispatch("app.start", AppStart(project_root=...), lambda e: None). Without a host, m.ui only logs, timers never fire and no client is reachable.

A mod shipped by an official plugin keeps its tests beside it; they run with the plugin's own suite.

docs.title: Shipping a mod with a plugin
docs.text:
An official plugin ships mods by overriding mods_path on its plugin class, returning the folder that holds one subfolder per mod:

@property
def mods_path(self) -> Optional[Path]:
    return Path(__file__).parent / "mods"

They load while the plugin is enabled, and the user can still switch any of them off. Add the mods' folder to testpaths in pyproject.toml, and document the mod in docs/plugins/<plugin>/overview.md.

docs.title: Verifying live
docs.text:
1. Run titan-dev --mod-dir <folder> and watch ~/.local/state/titan/logs/titan.log for mod_loaded, mod_load_failed or mod_hook_failed.
  2. Open the Mods screen (m on the home screen) to see the mod's status and switch its sections.
  3. Restart after every edit: mods load at start and Titan does not watch their folders.

docs.title: Writing a Workspace
docs.text:
A workspace is a folder with two files, the same shape as a mod:

~/.titan/workspaces/hello/
├── workspace.toml   # what it is, what it needs, which events it hooks, its options and sections
└── workspace.py     # register(w, on, options)

Read Writing a Mod first: a workspace uses the same handle, the same state, clock, keys, store, ai and workflows, the same element tree and the same options and sections. This page covers only what differs.

docs.title: A first workspace
docs.text:
# workspace.toml
[workspace]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
icon = "👋"
description = "A screen that counts the workflows run this session"
events = ["workflow.run"]

# workspace.py
from titan_cli.ui.elements import Box, Text


def register(w, on, options):
    w.state.set("runs", 0)

    w.ui.view(lambda width: Box(Text(f"{w.state.get('runs')} workflows run", bold=True)), title="Hello")
    w.on_start(lambda w: w.ui.dock("Hello", on_click=w.ui.open_workspace))

    @on("workflow.run")
    def count(w, e, next):
        try:
            return next(e)
        finally:
            if not e.nested:
                w.state.update("runs", lambda n: (n or 0) + 1)

Restart Titan: a "Hello" tile appears in the dock; it opens the screen and Esc goes back. Changing w.state redraws the screen.

docs.title: What differs from a mod
docs.text: Mod Workspace Entry point mod.toml + mod.py, register(on, options) workspace.toml + workspace.py, register(w, on, options) What it draws Panes, dock tile, home card (ui.render hook) One full screen: w.ui.view(fn, title) Handle m, given to every hook w, given to register; hooks get it as their first argument Config table [mods.<name>] [workspaces.<name>] Events app.start, workflow.run, step.call, ui.render, section.change workflow.run, step.call, section.change Run once the screen exists app.start hook w.on_start(fn) Listed in the Mods screen Yes No (edit ~/.titan/config.toml)

docs.title: The view
docs.text:
w.ui.view(fn, title=None) registers fn(width), which answers with an element tree for a screen width columns wide. Titan calls it again when the window is resized and whenever w.state changes, and patches what is on screen instead of redrawing it, so a focused button or a half-typed field survives. title heads the screen (it defaults to the workspace's name). fn reads w.state only: never the network or the disk.

For two columns that stack on a narrow window use responsive_columns, and keep any text field outside the columns:

from titan_cli.ui.elements import Box, responsive_columns

def view(width):
    return Box(
        search_field(),
        responsive_columns(width, [left, right], ratio=(3, 2), collapse_below=120),
    )

Each builder gets the width its column has, so a choice_card or a wrapped line fits either layout. The elements are in Writing a Mod.

docs.title: Starting and opening
docs.text:
register runs while Titan is still building, before there is a screen: a w.ui call there goes nowhere. Put what needs the screen (the dock tile, timers, keys) in w.on_start(fn), which runs fn(w) once the interface is up. w.ui.view is fine in register: it only stores the function.

w.on_open(fn) runs fn(w, focus) each time the screen is opened, before it draws. focus is whatever the opener passed to open_workspace(name, focus=...), None from the dock tile. A mod uses it to point you at the thing it listed:

# in the mod: pressing a PR opens the workspace on it
m.ui.open_workspace("github", focus={"pr": 42})

# in the workspace: unfold that row
def focus(w, what):
    if isinstance(what, dict) and what.get("pr"):
        w.state.update("rows_open", lambda rows: {**(rows or {}), str(what["pr"]): True}, default={})

w.on_open(focus)

open_workspace(name) returns False and shows a toast when there is no such workspace.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: A workspace hooks only the events its workspace.toml lists in events, with the on it receives, exactly as a mod does. A workspace's hooks wrap a workflow outside the mods' ones. app.start and ui.render are not available: use w.on_start and w.ui.view.

docs.title: Sharing code with a mod
docs.text: When a mod and a workspace read the same service, put the readers and the snapshots they build in an ordinary package of the plugin and import them from both; neither imports the other, and either may be switched off. The github plugin does it with titan_plugin_github/readers/.

docs.title: Where to put it
docs.text:
You want Put it in Yours, for every project ~/.titan/workspaces/<name>/ The team's, in one repo <repo>/.titan/workspaces/<name>/ Shipped with an official plugin the folder the plugin's workspaces_path returns Under development anywhere, then titan --workspace-dir <folder>

See Workspaces for the full order and the config.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Test the view as a pure function: build a ModBus(prefix="workspace.", store_dir="workspaces"), take bus.api(name), set w.state, call bus.render_view(name, width) and read the tree. import_mod(folder, kind=WORKSPACES) imports the folder exactly as Titan does. Run bus.start() to fire the w.on_start functions and bus.opened(name, focus) for w.on_open.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Coming soon

Detailed architecture documentation is being written. In the meantime, contributors can refer to the internal docs in .claude/docs/ within the repository.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Titan follows a 5-layer plugin architecture:

Steps → Operations → Client → Services → Network
  ↓         ↓          ↓         ↓          ↓
 UI    Business    Public   Data Access   HTTP/CLI
       Logic       API

Each official plugin (Git, GitHub, Jira) follows this structure. See the source in plugins/ for reference implementations.

docs.title: Plugin API Compatibility Rule
docs.text:
Everything importable under titan_cli.* is de-facto public API for plugins: community plugins run in-process and import Titan modules directly (plugin_base, config, security, step/workflow helpers, ...). Moving, renaming, or deleting any of those modules breaks every plugin release built against them — and the break only surfaces on users' machines, when their pinned plugin stops loading after a titan-cli upgrade.

When a change removes or relocates something plugins import:

  1. Keep the old import path working for at least one minor release, as a re-export or deprecated alias pointing at the new location. Delete it in the following minor.
  2. If a hard break is unavoidable, coordinate releases with the known plugin repos before shipping: each plugin needs a release that supports both APIs (import fallback) or, at minimum, a release with the new API plus a corrected titan-cli lower bound — published so projects can update the moment they upgrade titan-cli.
  3. Never assume plugins will "just update": projects pin plugin versions by commit, so an old pin plus a new titan-cli is a combination that will exist in the wild.

Runtime enforcement (do not weaken it): the registry checks each plugin's declared titan-cli requirement before importing it, translates ModuleNotFoundError on titan_cli.* imports into a version-incompatibility error, and the install/update flows refuse to pin a version whose requirement excludes the running titan-cli. Precedent: titan_cli.core.secrets → titan_cli.core.security (0.8.0) shipped without an alias and broke every pinned ragnarok plugin ≤ 0.10.0 on upgrade.

docs.title: Plugin Documentation Rule
docs.text:
When working on an official plugin, keep its public documentation in sync with the code.

This applies to changes in:

  • New public client functions
  • Removed public client functions
  • Parameter changes in existing public client functions
  • Behavioral changes that affect how an existing function should be used
  • New plugin workflows that expose new capabilities worth documenting

Update the corresponding page in the Plugins section:

  • Git Plugin
  • GitHub Plugin
  • Jira Plugin

At minimum, the documentation should reflect:

  • The operation name
  • How to call it
  • Which parameters are required
  • Which parameters are optional
  • Any important usage constraints

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text: This guide is for contributors who want to work on Titan CLI itself.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • Poetry for dependency management
  • Git
# Install Poetry if you don't have it
pipx install poetry

docs.title: Clone and install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/masorange/titan-cli.git
cd titan-cli

make dev-install

make dev-install does two things:

  1. Runs poetry install — creates a virtualenv at .venv/ with all dependencies, including the three plugins in editable mode
  2. Creates ~/.local/bin/titan-dev — a wrapper script that runs Titan from your local source

docs.title: Run your changes
docs.text:
titan-dev

titan-dev always runs from your local codebase. No reinstall needed after editing Python files.

docs.title: Logging in titan-dev
docs.text:
• titan-dev enables development logging.
  • During TUI execution, logs are written to ~/.local/state/titan/logs/titan.log.
  • If you want live visual debugging with Textual, run titan-dev --devtools and start textual console in another terminal.

Note

titan-dev is only for contributors. End users who install from PyPI get only the titan command.

docs.title: Run tests
docs.text:
make test
# or
poetry run pytest

The test suite covers the main package and all three plugins.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
titan-cli/
├── titan_cli/              # Core engine, TUI, CLI
│   ├── engine/            # Workflow execution
│   └── ui/tui/            # Textual TUI interface
├── plugins/
│   ├── titan-plugin-git/
│   ├── titan-plugin-github/
│   └── titan-plugin-jira/
├── tests/
└── pyproject.toml

Each plugin is an independent Python package installed in editable mode during development.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
To work on this documentation site locally:

make docs-serve

Opens a live-reloading preview at http://localhost:8000. Changes to any file in docs/ are reflected instantly.

docs.title: Public plugin step documentation
docs.text:
Official plugins expose a public workflow-step API through plugin.py -> get_steps().

When you add or change a public plugin step, you must update both code and docs:

  1. Update the step docstring using the canonical sections:
  2. Requires:
  3. Inputs (from ctx.data):
  4. Outputs (saved to ctx.data):
  5. Returns:
  6. Update the relevant pages under docs/plugins/
  7. Update the grouping metadata under docs/plugins/_meta/ if you add or rename a public step
  8. Regenerate and validate the machine-readable inventories under docs/plugins/_generated/

This repository maintains the generated inventory through project workflows in .titan/workflows/:

  • sync-plugin-docs
  • validate-plugin-docs

The generated inventories are not a replacement for the human-facing docs pages, but they are the source of truth for validation and consistency checks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or later
  • macOS, Linux, or Windows (WSL2 recommended on Windows)

docs.title: Install with pipx (recommended)
docs.text:
pipx installs Titan in an isolated environment and puts it on your PATH automatically — no virtualenv management needed.

# Install pipx if you don't have it
python3 -m pip install --user pipx
python3 -m pipx ensurepath

# Install Titan
pipx install titan-cli

Verify:

titan --version

docs.title: Install with pip
docs.text:
If you prefer a regular pip install into an existing environment:

pip install titan-cli

Warning

Using pip directly can create dependency conflicts with other packages. pipx is strongly recommended.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
Run Titan from inside a project directory:

cd /path/to/your-project
titan

On first launch, two setup wizards run automatically:

  1. Global setup — Configure AI connections. This is optional and can be skipped.
  2. Project setup — Choose a project name and enable the plugins you want (Git, GitHub, Jira).

After setup, the home screen appears with a grid of workflows you can launch by number — see Quick Start.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Path Purpose ~/.titan/config.toml Global config: AI connections and credentials .titan/config.toml Project config: enabled plugins and settings

The project config lives at the git repository root, so it works correctly in monorepos.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: → Quick Start — Learn the basics of the Titan interface.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide assumes Titan is already installed. If not, see Installation.

docs.title: Launch Titan
docs.text:
Run titan from inside any configured project:

cd /path/to/your-project
titan

Titan resolves the project root from the git repository root, so you can run it from any subdirectory of a monorepo.

docs.title: The home screen
docs.text:
After launch you land on the home screen: a grid of up to nine workflow cards, each one launchable by pressing its number.

⚡ Quick launch

╭─ ⭐ 1 ──────────────╮  ╭─ ⭐ 2 ──────────────╮  ╭─ 3 ─────────────────╮
│ Review PR          │  │ Commit with AI     │  │ Create Pull Request │
│ Github             │  │ Git                │  │ Github              │
│                    │  │                    │  │                     │
│ Focused AI review  │  │ Create a commit    │  │ AI-powered PR        │
│ for new findings   │  │ with AI message    │  │ creation             │
╰────────────────────╯  ╰────────────────────╯  ╰─────────────────────╯

  ⚡ All workflows [w]     🔌 Plugins [p]     🤖 AI [a]
Key Action 1–9 Run the workflow on that card Tab / Shift+Tab Move the focus between cards, then Enter to run the focused one w Open the full workflow list p Open plugin management a Open AI configuration q / Esc Quit

The cards reflow into fewer columns as the terminal gets narrower, down to one card per row. Which workflows are on the grid, and which number each one has, never changes with the window size — so a key you have learned keeps working at any width.

docs.title: How the nine slots are chosen
docs.text:
Slots are filled in this order, skipping anything already placed:

  1. Your favorites, in the order you starred them.
  2. Recently used workflows, most recent first.
  3. A balanced round-robin across workflow groups (Git, Github, Jira, Project, Personal…), one per group per pass, alphabetically — so a plugin with twenty workflows cannot crowd out the rest.

A card carrying a ⭐ is one you starred; the rest are suggestions Titan picked for you. That star is the only thing that distinguishes them — the heading above the grid deliberately says nothing about where the cards came from, because on a typical grid they come from both.

If no plugins are enabled there is no grid at all, just a prompt to open plugin management with p.

docs.title: Starring a workflow
docs.text:
Press f while a workflow is running, or click ☆ Favorite in that screen's header, to star it. The star is a toggle — press it again to remove it. Starred workflows move to the front of the grid, and the home screen picks the change up as soon as you return to it.

If you star more than nine workflows, the grid grows and scrolls to show all of them; the number keys serve the first nine, and the rest are marked with a star but no number.

Favorites and recent workflows are per project

Both are stored against the project's path, so starring a workflow in one repository does not put it on the home screen of another — even when both repositories have a workflow of the same name. Titan remembers the 20 most recently run workflows per project.

Where the cards come from:

  • Built-in plugin workflows (Git, GitHub, Jira)
  • Your project's own workflows in .titan/workflows/

docs.title: The full workflow list
docs.text: Press w for everything, not just the nine on the home screen. Filter by plugin in the left panel, then press Enter to run. Favorites are sorted to the top here too.

docs.title: Run a workflow
docs.text:
Workflows are interactive — they guide you through each step with prompts and confirmations.

For example, the Commit with AI workflow (from the Git plugin):

  1. Shows you the current git diff
  2. Lets you stage changes interactively
  3. Generates a commit message with AI (if configured)
  4. Lets you edit the message before committing

At any point you can press Escape or Ctrl+C to cancel.

docs.title: Enable or disable plugins
docs.text:
Edit .titan/config.toml in your project root:

[project]
name = "my-project"

[plugins.git]
enabled = true

[plugins.github]
enabled = true

[plugins.jira]
enabled = false

docs.title: Configure AI
docs.text:
Edit ~/.titan/config.toml:

[ai]
default_connection = "default"

[ai.connections.default]
name = "My Anthropic"
kind = "direct_provider"
provider = "anthropic"
default_model = "claude-sonnet-4-5"

Titan will prompt for your API key on first use and store it securely in your OS keyring.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: → Your First Workflow — Build a custom workflow from scratch.

docs.title: Your First Textual Step
docs.text:
In this tutorial you'll build a small project step that uses Titan's ctx.textual API so it looks consistent with built-in workflows.

You will learn how to:

  • write a project step in .titan/steps/
  • use ctx.textual.begin_step() and end_step()
  • ask the user for input and return metadata to later steps

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text: You want a small workflow that asks for a release name and saves it into workflow context so another step can use it later.

docs.title: Step 1 - Create the step file
docs.text:
Create .titan/steps/ask_release_name.py:

from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Error


def ask_release_name(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    if not ctx.textual:
        return Error("Textual UI context is not available for this step.")

    ctx.textual.begin_step("Release Name")

    try:
        name = ctx.textual.ask_text("Enter release name:")
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
        ctx.textual.end_step("error")
        return Error("User cancelled")

    if not name:
        ctx.textual.end_step("error")
        return Error("Release name is required")

    ctx.textual.success_text(f"Using release name: {name}")
    ctx.textual.end_step("success")
    return Success("Release name captured", metadata={"release_name": name})

Things to notice:

  • the function name ask_release_name must match the YAML step: value exactly
  • begin_step() and end_step() make the output look like Titan's built-in steps
  • ask_text() gives you a consistent prompt UI
  • metadata saves release_name for later steps

docs.title: Step 2 - Create a workflow
docs.text:
Create .titan/workflows/release-name-demo.yaml:

name: "Release Name Demo"
description: "Ask for a release name and show it"

steps:
  - id: ask-release-name
    name: "Ask Release Name"
    plugin: project
    step: ask_release_name

  - id: show-release-name
    name: "Show Release Name"
    command: "printf 'Release: %s\n' '${release_name}'"
    params:
      release_name: "${release_name}"

This workflow:

  • runs your project step first
  • stores release_name in workflow context
  • uses that value in a later step

docs.title: Step 3 - Run it
docs.text:
Launch Titan and run the new workflow from the menu.

You should see:

  • a step header for Release Name
  • a Textual prompt asking for the release name
  • a success message once the value is captured

docs.title: What to read next
docs.text:
• Workflow Steps
  • Textual in Steps
  • Workflows

docs.title: Your First Workflow
docs.text:
In this tutorial you'll build a custom workflow that runs a linter before every commit. You'll learn how to:

  • Write a custom step in Python
  • Extend a built-in workflow using hooks
  • Run your workflow from Titan

Prerequisites: Titan installed and configured in a project with the git plugin enabled. If not, see Installation.

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text:
The built-in commit-ai workflow commits your changes with an AI-generated message. You want to run ruff (a Python linter) before the commit happens, and skip it gracefully if ruff isn't installed.

You'll inject your linter step into the before_commit hook that commit-ai already exposes.

docs.title: Step 1 — Write the step function
docs.text:
Create the file .titan/steps/run_linter.py in your project:

import subprocess
from titan_cli.engine import WorkflowContext, WorkflowResult, Success, Skip, Error


def run_linter(ctx: WorkflowContext) -> WorkflowResult:
    """Run ruff linter. Skip gracefully if ruff is not installed."""

    # Check ruff is available
    check = subprocess.run(
        ["ruff", "--version"],
        capture_output=True,
    )
    if check.returncode != 0:
        return Skip("ruff not found — skipping lint")

    # Run the linter
    result = subprocess.run(
        ["ruff", "check", "."],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )

    if result.returncode != 0:
        ctx.textual.text(result.stdout)
        return Error("Linting failed — fix errors before committing")

    return Success("Linting passed")

A few things to notice:

  • The function name (run_linter) must match the step: field in the YAML exactly.
  • We return Skip when ruff isn't available — this lets the workflow continue without failing.
  • We return Error when lint fails — by default this stops the workflow (no commit happens).
  • We return Success when everything is fine.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create the workflow file
docs.text:
Create .titan/workflows/commit-ai.yaml:

name: "Commit with AI + Linter"
description: "Runs ruff before committing with an AI-generated message"
extends: "plugin:git/commit-ai"

hooks:
  before_commit:
    - id: run-lint
      name: "Run Linter"
      plugin: project
      step: run_linter
      on_error: continue   # remove this line if you want lint failures to block the commit

What this does:

  • extends: "plugin:git/commit-ai" — takes the base workflow from the git plugin
  • hooks.before_commit — injects your step at the before_commit injection point
  • plugin: project — tells Titan to look for run_linter in .titan/steps/
  • on_error: continue — even if linting fails, the commit step still runs (remove this to make lint failures block commits)

Because this file is named commit-ai.yaml and lives in .titan/workflows/, it overrides the built-in commit-ai workflow for this project. Titan's precedence rules mean project workflows always win.

docs.title: Step 3 — Run it
docs.text:
titan

Select Commit with AI + Linter from the menu. The workflow runs your lint step before generating the commit message.

You'll see each step in the TUI as it executes. If linting fails (and you kept on_error: continue), you'll see the lint errors but the commit step will still run. Remove that line to make lint failures stop the workflow.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
You've seen the two core building blocks: a step (Python function) and a workflow (YAML that sequences steps). From here you can:

  • Add more steps to .titan/steps/ and wire them into workflows
  • Create a completely new workflow (no extends) for project-specific automation
  • Use ctx.get() and metadata to pass data between steps
  • Add AI calls using ctx.ai for generated content

Read Workflow Concepts for the full reference on step types, result types, parameters, and the Skip vs Exit distinction.

If you want your custom steps to use Titan's TUI API directly, continue with Your First Textual Step.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Titan exposes plugin capabilities through three public layers:

  • Client API: Python entry points used from Titan code.
  • Workflow Steps: reusable step functions exposed through plugin.get_steps().
  • Built-in Workflows: YAML workflows shipped by each plugin.

This section documents official plugins from those three angles so users can both call plugin clients directly and compose workflows from reusable public steps.

docs.title: Official plugins
docs.text:
Titan ships with five official plugins:

Plugin Description git Smart commits, branch management, AI-powered commit messages github Create PRs with AI descriptions, manage issues, code reviews jira Search issues, AI-powered analysis, workflow automation slack Personal Slack auth, workspace summaries, and reusable Slack workflow steps docker Docker Compose lifecycle management and image build/push workflows

Enable them per project in .titan/config.toml:

[plugins.git]
enabled = true

[plugins.github]
enabled = true

[plugins.jira]
enabled = true

[plugins.slack]
enabled = true

[plugins.docker]
enabled = true

For each plugin, the docs are split into:

  • Overview: requirements, configuration, and entry points.
  • Client API: public client methods grouped by domain.
  • Workflow Steps: public reusable steps grouped by functionality.
  • Built-in Workflows: workflows shipped by the plugin and how to extend them.

docs.title: Community plugins
docs.text:
Titan also supports community plugins from external repositories.

There are currently two source channels:

  • stable: pin a plugin version in the project config using a git tag or commit.
  • dev_local: use a local checkout of a plugin repository during development.

The shared stable pin lives in .titan/config.toml:

[plugins.custom]
enabled = true

[plugins.custom.source]
channel = "stable"
repo_url = "https://github.com/user/titan-plugin-custom"
requested_ref = "v1.2.0"
resolved_commit = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"

requested_ref stores the exact tag or ref used by that repository. Some repos use tags like v1.2.0; others use 1.2.0.

For local plugin development, the active override lives in ~/.titan/config.toml:

[plugins.custom.source]
channel = "dev_local"
path = "/absolute/path/to/local/plugin/repo"

In dev_local, Titan loads the plugin directly from the local repository. In stable, Titan prepares a local runtime for the pinned commit: a checkout plus a virtualenv with the plugin's dependencies.

docs.title: Declaring dependencies
docs.text:
A plugin runs inside Titan's own interpreter. Its virtualenv supplies libraries Titan does not ship; it does not isolate the plugin, and it never overrides what Titan already has:

The library is... Which version the plugin gets Not shipped by Titan (e.g. PyJWT) The plugin's own, from its runtime Also shipped by Titan (e.g. requests) Titan's, whatever the plugin pinned

So pin ranges compatible with what Titan ships. A plugin that needs a conflicting major version of a shared library cannot be satisfied today.

titan-cli is a special case: it is the host, not a dependency to install. Titan is already running when it loads your plugin. Declare it as optional, so installing the plugin never places a second copy of Titan — and of the official plugins that come with it — inside the plugin's runtime:

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
titan-cli = {version = ">=0.9.0,<1.0.0", optional = true, python = ">=3.11"}

[tool.poetry.extras]
# Only for working on the plugin repo itself: `poetry install --extras host`.
host = ["titan-cli"]

Keep the declaration, though: the version range is the compatibility contract Titan reads before loading your plugin (see below). Removing it does not make your plugin more compatible — it just turns the check off.

docs.title: Version compatibility
docs.text:
A plugin is built against the Titan plugin API of a specific titan-cli range. When the two drift apart — a project pinned to an old plugin version after upgrading titan-cli, or updating a plugin beyond what the installed titan-cli supports — the plugin cannot load. Titan detects this in both directions:

  • Declared contract. The plugin's pyproject.toml dependency on titan-cli is the compatibility contract. Titan checks it before loading a plugin, before installing one, and before applying an update — an update whose target version requires a different titan-cli is rejected with a message telling you which side to upgrade, instead of leaving a broken pin.
  • Fallback detection. If a plugin with loose bounds imports a titan_cli.* module that does not exist in the running titan-cli, the failure is reported as a version incompatibility ("update the plugin"), not as a generic crash.

An incompatible or crashed plugin appears as Load failed in Plugin Management, with the reason in the details panel. A failed plugin with a stable pin can still be updated from there (the pin lives in the project config, not in the plugin), so a broken pinned version is never a dead end.

For plugin authors:

  • Declare an accurate titan-cli bound and keep it honest, e.g. titan-cli = ">=0.8.0,<0.9". A bound like >=0.6.0 promises compatibility with every future titan-cli, which no plugin can keep; without a real upper bound only the fallback detection protects your users.
  • When migrating to a renamed or moved titan-cli API, prefer a release that supports both APIs (try: import new / except ImportError: import old) so projects can upgrade titan-cli and the plugin in either order. Drop the shim, and raise the lower bound, one release later.
  • Bump your plugin's MAJOR (or clearly flag the release) when a version stops supporting a titan-cli range that the previous release supported.

docs.title: Docker Client API
docs.text:
The Docker plugin adds Docker Compose lifecycle management and image build/push operations to Titan through a high-level client and reusable workflows.

This page documents the plugin from a functional point of view, while also showing how each capability is called and which parameters it needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
To use the Docker plugin in a project:

  • Enable the docker plugin in .titan/config.toml
  • Install Docker (with the compose and buildx CLI plugins) and make sure it is available in PATH

Example project configuration:

[plugins.docker]
enabled = true

[plugins.docker.config]
compose_file = "docker-compose.yml"

[plugins.docker.config.service_groups]
infra = ["db", "cache"]

[[plugins.docker.config.build_targets]]
name = "backend"
dockerfile = "packages/backend/Dockerfile"
context = "."
image = "ghcr.io/org/app-backend"
target = "production"
push = true

docs.title: Accessing the client
docs.text:
In Titan code, the public entry point is the Docker plugin client:

docker_plugin = config.registry.get_plugin("docker")
client = docker_plugin.get_client()

The client returns ClientResult[...] values. In practice, this means each call can succeed with data or return an error result.

The client also carries the project's configured service_groups and build_targets as plain attributes (client.service_groups, client.build_targets), so steps and operations can resolve them without a separate config lookup.

docs.title: Start services
docs.text:
Starts compose services in the background.

Call:

client.compose_up(services=["db", "cache"])

Parameters:

  • services (list of str, optional): Service names to start. Omit or pass an empty list to start every service in the compose file.
  • detach (bool, optional): Run containers in the background. Defaults to True.

docs.title: Stop services
docs.text:
Stops compose services.

Call:

client.compose_down(services=["db", "cache"])

Parameters:

  • services (list of str, optional): Service names to stop. Omit or pass an empty list to stop (down) the whole project; a non-empty list runs stop on just those services.

docs.title: Get compose status
docs.text:
Returns the state of compose services (running/exited, health, status text).

Call:

client.compose_status(services=["db"])

Parameters:

  • services (list of str, optional): Service names to inspect. Omit or pass an empty list to inspect every service.

docs.title: Build (and optionally push) an image
docs.text:
Builds a single configured image with docker buildx build, covering both single-platform and multi-platform builds through the same code path.

Call:

from titan_cli.core.plugins.models import DockerBuildTargetConfig

target = DockerBuildTargetConfig(
    name="backend",
    dockerfile="packages/backend/Dockerfile",
    context=".",
    image="ghcr.io/org/app-backend",
    target="production",
    platforms="linux/amd64",
    tag="latest",
    push=True,
)
client.build_target(target)

# Stream build output line by line instead of waiting for the final result
client.build_target(target, on_output=lambda line: print(line))

Parameters:

  • target (DockerBuildTargetConfig, required): the build target to build. Typically resolved from client.build_targets (project configuration) rather than constructed by hand. When its platforms is unset, no --platform flag is passed and buildx builds for the builder's native platform (see Build target fields).
  • on_output (callable, optional): called with each line of docker buildx build output as it streams (stdout+stderr merged, in emission order). Omit to just run the build and get the final result.

docs.title: Prune operations
docs.text: These operate on the whole Docker host, not just this project - Docker doesn't scope disk usage or prune targets to a single compose file.

docs.title: Get disk usage
docs.text:
Returns a breakdown of Docker's disk usage (images, containers, local volumes, build cache) via docker system df.

Call:

client.disk_usage()

Parameters:

  • No parameters.

docs.title: Prune resources
docs.text:
Removes unused resources for the given categories.

Call:

client.prune(["containers", "images"])

Parameters:

  • targets (list of str, required): subset of "containers", "images", "build_cache", "volumes". "images" only removes dangling (untagged) images. Docker itself refuses to remove a volume still attached to any container, so "volumes" never touches an in-use volume.

docs.title: Container operations
docs.text: These also operate on the whole Docker host - every container, not just this project's compose services.

docs.title: List containers
docs.text:
Lists every container on the host, running or stopped.

Call:

client.list_containers()

Parameters:

  • No parameters.

docs.title: Remove containers
docs.text:
Removes the given containers via docker rm (without -f).

Call:

client.remove_containers(["abc123", "def456"])

Parameters:

  • container_ids (list of str, required): container IDs or names to remove. Docker itself refuses (surfaced as a ClientError) if any of them is still running.

docs.title: Docker Plugin
docs.text:
The Docker plugin provides Titan's Docker Compose lifecycle and image build/push surface. It exposes:

  • a high-level DockerClient for direct use from Titan code
  • reusable workflow steps such as compose_up, compose_status, and build_push_images
  • the built-in docker-up and docker-build-push workflows

The plugin has no built-in notion of any specific project's services or images: service_groups (named groups of compose service names) and build_targets (buildable images) are entirely defined by each project's .titan/config.toml.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
To use the Docker plugin in a project:

  • Enable the docker plugin in .titan/config.toml
  • Install Docker (with the compose and buildx CLI plugins) and make sure it is available in PATH

Example project configuration:

[plugins.docker]
enabled = true

[plugins.docker.config]
compose_file = "docker-compose.yml"

[plugins.docker.config.service_groups]
infra = ["db", "cache"]

[[plugins.docker.config.build_targets]]
name = "backend"
dockerfile = "packages/backend/Dockerfile"
context = "."
image = "ghcr.io/org/app-backend"
target = "production"
platforms = "linux/amd64"
push = true

docs.title: Build target fields
docs.text: Field Required Default Description name yes - Unique name for the target within the project (also what docker-build-push accepts to build a single image) dockerfile yes - Path to the Dockerfile, relative to the project root image yes - Image reference to build/push, without tag (e.g. ghcr.io/org/app-backend) context no "." Build context path, relative to the project root target no none Dockerfile build stage to target (e.g. production) platforms no builder native Comma-separated --platform list for buildx tag no "latest" Tag applied to the built image push no false Push to the registry after building

docs.title: About platforms
docs.text:
When platforms is omitted, the plugin passes no --platform flag and buildx builds for the builder's native platform.

Set it explicitly when the deploy target differs from the machine doing the build (e.g. platforms = "linux/amd64" on an arm64 laptop deploying to an amd64 server), or to publish a multi-arch image (platforms = "linux/amd64,linux/arm64").

Every platform in the list that the build host does not natively match is built under QEMU emulation, which costs a full slow build per platform - dependencies are recompiled or re-downloaded for that architecture. Only list architectures you actually deploy.
